https://www.politico.eu/article/serbia-l.text: Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has dissolved his country’s parliament and announced snap elections for the end of October as he seeks to assert control over the febrile political situation in the country. “I am convinced that the citizens of Serbia will choose the right path into the future,” Vučić said Wednesday, adding that “preserving our democratic system” and avoiding divisions were his priorities. The snap elections will take place on Oct. 25, according to reports in Serbian media . Vučić acknowledged “turbulence” in Serbian society but blamed “significant interference by foreign powers” for inspiring student-led anti-corruption protests that have fueled the country’s political turmoil over the past two years. Advertisement Advertisement Demonstrations erupted after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024 , killing 16 people. Protestors have demanded accountability over the disaster and called for early parliamentary elections. On Monday, Prime Minister Đuro Macut asked Vučić to dissolve parliament and call fresh elections. “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people,” Macut said . Vučić, who has been in power as ‌president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced calls to step down since the 2023 parliamentary elections, amid allegations of electoral fraud. His second and final term as president is set to end in 2027 and his powers will not expire with the dissolution of parliament. In June, Vučić said he would resign as president “within weeks,” but his ambitions to remain in power continue. His Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) has nominated him for prime minister if the party secures a majority in the upcoming snap election. Serbia has been a candidate for EU membership since 2012, but its bid has stalled over concerns about democratic backsliding in Belgrade and its refusal to sanction Russia for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

http://www.australiannews.net/news/27934.text: Home Asia Pacific News International News Business News Search News Network As Russia Tests Western Alliance, US Lawmakers Push NATO Shield Bill RFE 03 Oct 2026, 04:43 GMT+ WASHINGTON -- As tensions between NATO and Russia intensify amid growing fears of confrontation, US lawmakers are raising questions over the relationship between the United States and the military alliance. That is the issue at the center of a new bipartisanbillled by Democratic lawmaker Jimmy Panetta and his Republican counterpart Joe Wilson. TheNATO Shield Actwould require congressional approval before a president could initiate a US withdrawal from NATO. SEE ALSO: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans Panetta, in an interview with RFE/RL on October 1, argued that the measure is particularly important at a moment when Russia is testing the alliance and uncertainty surrounds Washington's future force posture in Europe. The legislation, introduced September 24, would require the president to consult Congress within 72 hours of considering a withdrawal from the military alliance and submit a report explaining the legal basis, strategic rationale, and expected consequences. Any withdrawal action would end after 30 days unless Congress approved it. Panetta said NATO is one of the most consequential and successful security alliances in the history of the world and argued that any fundamental change in US national security policy should not be left to the president to decide. But his argument goes beyond the possibility of a formal US withdrawal. Panetta said Russian President Vladimir Putin is already testing NATO through pressure, probing, and poking at the alliance before any potential move toward direct confrontation. He pointed to Russia's activities around the Baltic region, Poland, and other NATO border states as examples of what he described as gray-zone warfare. For Panetta, the danger lies partly in actions that remain below the threshold of open war. We cannot let gray-zone warfare go unnoticed and unresponded to, he said, warning that Russia could gradually pressure NATO members in much the same way China has applied pressure around Taiwan. An attack on one of us will be an attack on all, Panetta said, invoking the alliance's collective-defense principle laid out in Article 5 in NATO's founding treaty. https://www.novinite.com/articles/241351.text: iNews Novinite Econ DoctorOnline Jenite Div Sporta FitWell Sportuvai Peika Programata News in English BUSINESS POLITICS WORLD SOCIETY SPORTS Latest Culture Crime · Hotels 5* · Hotels 4* · Hotels 3* · Apartment Houses · Bar&Restaurants · Rent-a-car · Casino · Sport · Mountain resorts · Sea resorts · Education · Entertainment · Shopping · Health Clinics · Beauty Zone · Public Safety · Business Finance Best in BG Novinite Insider · Radisson Blu · 4 Seasons · French Survey · Investors Survey · Austrian Survey · Italian Survey · US Survey · Greek Survey · Dutch Survey Special Topics Editorial Interview Features Opinions Expert Voices Diplomatic Channel A Tired Debate, a Clear Divide: Why Sunday’s Runoff Is About Bulgaria’s Place in Europe Tweet Share Send to Kindle In Thursday night’s debate on the Bulgarian National Television, the only one before Sunday’s runoff, Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov were asked about the war next door. “Peace can only be achieved through negotiations,” Yotova said. “Russia cannot be excluded from this process.” For the Black Sea, where drones have hit five merchant ships in Bulgaria ’s economic zone this month, she proposed a meeting of the six littoral states, Russia among them, to agree a moratorium on hostilities. Gyurov ’s reply was shorter. “A moratorium, expressed merely as a wish, does not constitute a defense strategy. Silence is not defense.” He asked her to call the aggressor state by its name and then: “Did you call Putin to ask him to stop the war?” That exchange captured what Sunday’s runoff has become. Presidential elections in Bulgaria are usually fought over domestic grievances, above all corruption and the cost of living. This one started that way. By its final week, Rumen Radev’s government had told voters the runoff was a choice “between peace and war,” refused to name Russia over the Black Sea strikes and hinted that Romania had invited further attacks by doing so. On Thursday, the two candidates gave opposite answers to the question Radev had posed. What the Debate Showed It was not a memorable night for either candidate. Both looked tired, with Yotova on the attack for most of the two hours and Gyurov on the defensive, replying with reasoned but brief and low-energy answers, as if Gyurov were the incumbent and Yotova the ambitious opposition figure. Neither landed a knockout blow. The substance, though, was unusually clear. Yotova filled out her position with history and diplomacy. She argued that sending more weapons to Ukraine only adds to the casualties, that the war began in 2013 and 2014 and not in 2022, and that Russia cannot be brought to the table through ultimatums. Gyurov said the Black Sea “has become more insecure than the Persian Gulf,” the result of “a policy of appeasement,” and that an aggressor stops only “when the cost of an attack becomes prohibitively high.” On Bulgaria ’s place in Europe he put it more bluntly still: “If you aren’t at the table, you’re on the menu.” The debate also exposed where each candidate stands toward the government. Asked by moderator Poli Zlatareva whether she would uphold the policies of the government and Progressive Bulgaria from the presidency, Yotova would not answer, suggesting the question was a talking point of “the people who nominated Gyurov.” Gyurov said he was “an independent candidate” with “no connection” to the parties supporting him. The claim is generous to himself, since he chaired We Continue the Change’s parliamentary group and runs with the backing of PP, DB and the DSB. But he answered the question, and she did not, and it matters because of what an aligned presidency would be aligned with. Her other answers suggested what that alignment would look like. She said she would sign the government's next budget "even if, through some very unfortunate turn of events, you were to win," which is accurate, since her current term runs until January 2027. She called for scrapping the restricted list of caretaker prime ministers, echoing a proposal Radev's government announced in August. Asked about a deputy prime minister who divides the press into "good" and "bad" media while the government's press office campaigns for her, she replied that freedom of the media means freedom of opinion "for the Deputy Prime Minister, for the Prime Minister, and for everyone else." Several of her claims do not survive a check. She said the deal with Turkey's Botas came about because "Kiril Petkov and Asen Vassilev cut off Russian gas supplies to Bulgaria overnight." In fact Gazprom halted deliveries in April 2022 after Sofia refused to pay in rubles, and the Botas agreement was signed in January 2023 by the caretaker government of Galab Donev, whom Radev appointed. Bulgaria has since come to owe Botas hundreds of millions of dollars. She presented Gyurov 's security agreement with Ukraine as a commitment to send Bulgarian soldiers as peacekeepers, but Radev himself told parliament that the agreement contains no commitment to specific actions and his government has not terminated it. And when Gyurov argued that Bulgaria should shape EU decisions instead of waiting to veto them, Yotova said she could not recall a single Bulgarian veto, although Sofia blocked the start of North Macedonia's EU accession talks from late 2020, with Radev's backing, the very dispute the two argued over minutes later. Gyurov was not immune either. His suggestion that the arrests of DPS mayors were the result of a broken deal between Progressive Bulgaria and DPS is speculation for which he offered no evidence. Yotova , in turn, accused him of describing the arrests as a new "Revival Process," the communist-era campaign against Bulgarian Turks, which he denied ever saying, and she cited no source. Former prime minister Kiril Petkov, whose government Yotova attacked over the French proposal on North Macedonia, responded after the debate that it was his cabinet that turned the veto into the French proposal backed by the whole EU, that his trip to Skopje with Yotova had been for the opening of a friendship club, unrelated to the negotiations, and that it was Russia that cut off gas supplies. Petkov is a partisan voice, but on Gazprom the record bears him out. If the government wants this vote to be about where Bulgaria stands in the world, voters are entitled to take the question seriously. The answer the evidence points to is that Bulgaria 's security lies with its allies in the European Union and NATO and that the presidency should be held by someone willing to say so clearly. How the Governing Camp Reframed the Vote The shift began the morning after the first round, when Yotova 's 20-point poll lead had shrunk to 2.8 points in the actual count. Speaking at the Sofia Economic Forum on October 26, Radev framed the runoff as a choice between peace and war and urged voters to "send the 'assembly' to oblivion," his term for the coalition of GERB, DPS and PP-DB that preceded his government. He accused Andrey Gyurov of entering the race to protect Delyan Peevski and the official page of Progressive Bulgaria has since claimed that Gyurov met Peevski, which Gyurov calls a lie and for which no evidence has been offered. The message went out through the Council of Ministers' official channels. When Gyurov 's team complained to the Central Election Commission , the government's press office responded by instructing media to report the prime minister's words accurately, prompting the Association of European Journalists in Bulgaria to warn of conditions for censorship. A government that uses the state's machinery to tell voters that one candidate means war has no grounds to complain when the vote is read as a referendum on its foreign policy. The online campaign has followed the same pattern. A Sensika Technologies report on the campaign's social media found coordinated, artificially amplified activity on both sides: a network of Facebook groups with about 320,000 members, built around Nikolay Barekov and the BNews site, was renamed to back Yotova at the end of August, while anonymous TikTok "resistance" accounts posted 544 videos praising Gyurov. In neither case did the researchers find a direct link to the official campaigns. The report also found the Russian network Rybar presenting Radev and Yotova as a "stability factor" and identical texts circulating between Revival-linked Telegram groups and channels tied to Russian networks, though it cautions that timing alone does not prove coordination. Who Has Lined Up Behind Whom The endorsements of the past four days tell their own story. Behind Yotova stand Progressive Bulgaria , the Bulgarian Socialist Party and Georgi Parvanov's ABV. On October 28 Ivelin Mihaylov of Greatness, who finished fifth with 57,643 votes, called on his supporters to vote for her, describing it as a step toward "a change in governance" and insisting it was no choice of the lesser evil. Revival's Kostadin Kostadinov has stopped short of a formal endorsement, but he ruled out Gyurov entirely, promising that "Andrey Gyurov will not receive a single vote from Revival" and predicting that his voters would split between Yotova , abstention and the "I do not support anyone" box. In the same briefing he complained that the European Council had blamed Russia for the Black Sea attacks without evidence, and after the latest strike he suggested the targeted ship had "probably carried weapons," again without evidence. He told BGNES that Revival voters might have acted differently had Yotova formally asked for their support, and in the same remarks announced that he would travel to Moscow for a BRICS-related meeting where he is due to meet Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chair of Russia's Security Council, once again. The Party of European Socialists has endorsed Yotova , which led Ivaylo Mirchev of Yes, Bulgaria to ask how she squares that with tacit backing from a party that sits alongside Germany's AfD in the European Parliament. Gyurov has the support of We Continue the Change, Democratic Bulgaria and the DSB, and a deputy chair of the Union of Democratic Forces has called for a vote for him. MECH's Radostin Vassilev has not formally endorsed Gyurov either, though on election night he told his voters that they should vote "under no circumstances for Iliana Yotova ," adding: "In other words, they either vote for Andrey Gyurov or stay home." GERB and DPS have said nothing. Political analyst Berkay Chokdzhan argued on Bulgarian National Radio that both kept their voters at home in the first round to measure their electoral weight, and he doubts the arrests of DPS mayors were the main reason for the boycott. A candidate is not responsible for everyone who votes for them. Still, a camp that now gathers the parties most reluctant to name Russia as the aggressor in the Black Sea has defined itself, whether Yotova intended it or not. The Black Sea Paradox Nothing captures the governing camp's position better than Radev's remark about Romania. At the same forum on October 26 he said that Romania had pointed to Russia as the force behind the drone strikes and that new attacks on ships in Romanian waters had followed. Damyana Veleva of Svobodna Tochka summed up the logic with a schoolyard image: you point at the bully, and your neighbor scolds you for causing the next fight because you did not keep quiet. In Romania, the reaction ranged from former interim prime minister Cătălin Predoiu's call for "consistency, logic and mutual solidarity" to commentator Cosmin Prelipceanu's verdict on Digi24 that the remark was "pure delirium." The paradox is plain. Romania, where ships were sunk and sailors died off Constanța, is cast as partly responsible for naming the aggressor, while the aggressor goes unnamed. If accusing Russia provokes Russia, then Sofia already knows who is behind the attacks and has chosen not to say so. Radev has instead cited Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who, by his account, assured him she had no information that the drones were Russian. The policy has not even bought Bulgaria the quiet it implies. On October 28 the container ship Contship Jet, bound for Constanța, was hit by three sea drones about 17 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra, the fifth attack in Bulgaria 's own economic zone this month. A French patrol aircraft spotted it. Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov said the drones could not be intercepted because the attack took place outside Bulgarian territorial waters. Romania, meanwhile, has used F-16s to shoot down drones over its territory and summoned Russia's ambassador, and its new foreign minister, Dan Neculaescu, called the strikes a deliberate escalation in violation of international law. Sofia has asked allies for patrol aircraft, and that help is welcome, but it still will not name the threat that Bucharest has named. The pattern extends onshore. On October 9, eight of the 18 antennas at a Starlink ground station near Sofia that supports Ukraine's defense were set on fire . Two 19-year-old German citizens were arrested in Duisburg on October 23, and Lithuanian prosecutors, who have charged them over a similar attempt in Vilnius, are examining possible links to Russia. Ivaylo Mirchev of Yes, Bulgaria says a partner intelligence service warned Sofia at least a week in advance, a claim the government has not confirmed. Radev chose to brief journalists instead of answering in parliament. The Case for Yotova and Its Limits Yotova 's supporters have a case, and it deserves a fair hearing. Bulgaria is a small country next to a war and caution has real value. Insisting on evidence before blaming a nuclear power is defensible diplomacy, and a president who promises that no Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine speaks to a fear that many voters genuinely hold. After five years of political chaos, there is also something to be said for a head of state who works with the government instead of against it. The trouble is that caution has become an excuse for passivity. The pledge on soldiers addresses a decision that belongs to parliament, which already ruled out participation in the fighting in February 2025, so it protects voters from a danger nobody proposed. The demand for proof has hardened into a refusal to draw the conclusion that Bulgaria 's own allies, including the European Council and the government in Bucharest, have already drawn. And the language of peace has done nothing to stop ships burning off Kaliakra. Bulgaria 's security in the Black Sea depends on Romanian coordination, French aircraft and NATO assets, and every hint that the victims brought the attacks on themselves makes that help harder to keep. Gyurov 's Answer Gyurov 's reply came in a video address this week. "While those in power frighten us with war, it is precisely their inaction that allows the war to reach our shores," he said. "The government cannot, does not know how to and fails to protect its citizens." He accused Radev and Yotova of acting as observers who "do not inform the population, hide and refuse to take clear action," and dismissed Progressive Bulgaria 's claim about a meeting with Peevski as "desperate lies." Not every line was measured. Comparing the government's use of the word "warmongers" to the vocabulary of Goebbels and Stalin is the kind of escalation his campaign should leave to others. The substance, though, has been consistent. After the October 13 strikes he called for consultations under Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which means talks among allies and no military commitment. He has argued for working with Romania and Turkey and for using EU and NATO mechanisms to protect shipping, and on Ukraine he speaks of support for a lasting peace backed by security guarantees. A fabricated quote claiming he would send Bulgarian troops to Ukraine was debunked by Factcheck.bg . His central promise is modest and that is its strength.
